title: JavaScript Jam Live Meets React Miami: How a Community Open Mic Became a Game Show
outline: Opening: when live tech community goes sideways, then finds its rhythm
What JavaScript Jam Live actually is, and why the open-mic format still matters
The React Miami collaboration and why media partners were given a long leash
Meet the people on the call: Edgio, organizers, and fellow media partners
Miami Jam: replacing the usual speaker interview with trivia, quirks, and scorekeeping
How the format still gets to talks, motivation, and industry experience
Audience participation as a feature, not a courtesy
Beginners, veterans, and why the hosts keep the door open
What to expect next week and throughout React Miami Month
Closing: more value, same vibe, extra goodies
draft:
Live community audio is rarely elegant on the first try. JavaScript Jam Live opened this session with a Twitter Spaces hiccup that will feel painfully familiar to anyone who has ever hosted: the room looked live on one phone and invisible to everyone else. Scott got it working. Anthony recognized the pattern immediately. Sometimes a Space appears to start on the host device while remaining closed to the rest of the world, and after a minute or two it simply resolves. Patience, they joked, was a virtue. Then they did what good community hosts do. They thanked people for rejoining, introduced themselves, and got on with the show.

That small mess is a useful way into what this gathering actually is. JavaScript Jam Live is an open mic for JavaScript and web development. If it touches the web platform, it is on topic. The hosts want audience participation. They want beginners as much as they want people who have been shipping for a decade. They want questions, comments, opinions, and the kind of unplanned conversation that only happens when listeners request the mic. Scott Steinlage, technical community manager at Edgio, put it plainly: involvement raises the value for everyone listening. Great conversations tend to start when the room is not a broadcast.

This particular episode sat at the start of a longer collaboration with React Miami. Ishan Anand, VP of Product at Edgio, framed the week and the weeks after it as something special. Anthony Campolo, a developer advocate at Edgio, brought the same energy. Scott, hustling to get the Space live, even slipped and called it React Miami Week before correcting himself on air. He renamed it React Miami Month in real time. The point was not branding. The point was duration. This would not be a single guest drop. Speakers from React Miami would keep showing up on JavaScript Jam to talk about topics that fit the conference and still fit the show’s existing vibe. Nothing about the usual format was supposed to disappear. The partnership was meant to add value and, later, some extra goodies the hosts were clearly excited to unpack.

The people on the call mattered because the partnership is personal. Dev Agrawal joined as a media partner for React Miami, working alongside Anthony and Scott. He answered to Dev or Dave, both fine. Michelle, one of the organizers of React Miami, made it onto the Space after fighting the same platform friction: a flaky connection, a microphone button that refused to cooperate, the ordinary chaos of Twitter Spaces. She was, in her own words, kind of crashing the party, and she was also listening closely. The organizers had given the media partners a green light to do whatever they liked. Anthony could not resist a joke about whether she would regret that. The joke landed because the freedom was real. Michelle was interested in seeing what they would actually build with it.

Dan hopped up too, then immediately disqualified himself from a formal introduction. He had a company offsite the week of the conference. He wished he were going. He was not a media partner. The exchange was short and human, the kind of thing an open mic absorbs without ceremony. Will appeared as well. The room kept filling while the agenda found its shape.

The shape they wanted was not another interview hour. Dev had, as he put it, managed to rope Anthony and Scott into hosting a game show with him. They are calling it Miami Jam. It happens next week. The idea is to step away from the default conference-adjacent format: a few speakers, a few questions about their talks, a polite panel, a fade to credits. Miami Jam is trivia-first. Questions can be React-related. They can be about weird quirks in JavaScript or TypeScript or anything adjacent to React. They can ask someone to guess which library is in play. They can even send a question about another speaker’s topic to a person who then has to answer it. The trivia is not a gimmick bolted onto a serious conversation. It is the on-ramp.

That distinction is the heart of the experiment. Dev was careful to say they still get insight. They still hear what a speaker’s topic is, why they chose to give that talk, what their experience in the industry has been, and what they have built that brings them to React Miami. The structure simply changes how those answers arrive. A trivia miss can become a story. A correct answer can become a tangent about a library’s history. A question aimed at one speaker about another speaker’s work can force a little cross-talk, which is exactly the point. The hosts want speakers sharing experiences with each other, not only performing toward the audience. They want the hour to feel collaborative and engaging rather than extractive.

Audience members are not spectators in this design. If you are in the room, you still get to ask questions. You may also score them. Dev described a mechanic where a listener can decide how many points a speaker gets for an answer. The transcript cuts off as he starts to explain a question-about-question case, but the intention is already clear. Points, guesses, and audience judgment are there to make the show bidirectional. A typical interview lets the crowd clap at the end. A game show lets the crowd change the temperature of the room while it is still happening.

That matches the older JavaScript Jam habit of treating participation as load-bearing. Scott’s invitation was not a formality. Beginner or advanced, new to web development or years in, request the mic. Facts, opinions, half-formed comments, all of it. The hosts have learned that when people come up, the conversation gets better for the silent majority as well. Miami Jam is trying to keep that muscle while adding conference speakers, conference topics, and a scoring layer that gives listeners a job besides listening.

There is also a practical honesty running through the Space that is worth keeping in a write-up like this. Tech communities like to pretend they are smooth. This one admitted the opposite. Scott noted that it does not matter how much you know; something will still make you look foolish. Anthony had a ready story about Spaces that lie about being live. Michelle’s mic failed. Dev’s phone notifications interrupted him until he silenced the device. Dan could not make the conference because of work. These are not outtakes. They are the texture of an open mic that is trying to stay an open mic even while it partners with a destination conference.

React Miami, from this conversation, is not being treated as a content farm. The media partners are using the conference as a reason to gather speakers, then refusing to run those speakers through the most efficient interview template. Efficiency would be a short bio, three questions about the talk title, a plug for the schedule, and a goodbye. Miami Jam trades some of that efficiency for play. Play is riskier. Trivia can fall flat. Scoring can feel arbitrary. A question about a JavaScript quirk can eat five minutes that might have gone to a prepared anecdote. The bet is that the risk is the value. People remember a game they helped judge. They remember a speaker who missed a TypeScript oddity and then explained the production bug it once caused. They remember being asked to award points.

For attendees and remote listeners, the collaboration also means a calendar, not a one-off. More React Miami speakers will appear on JavaScript Jam around topics that make sense for them. The traditional vibe stays. The open-mic posture stays. The extra value is access: more voices from the conference, a game show that is allowed to be weird, and later surprises the hosts were not ready to spoil in the first few minutes. Scott’s “React Miami Month” line is the right mental model. Treat it as a stretch of programming, not a single night.

If you are a speaker, the format asks something slightly different of you. You may still talk about your talk. You may still explain your motivation. You will probably do it after a question that looks like a quiz. You may have to answer something about someone else’s session. You may have the audience deciding your points. That can feel exposing. It can also feel like a room instead of a keynote tunnel. If you are a listener, the ask is simpler and harder: come up. Ask. Score. Do not wait until you have a perfect question. The hosts already said they want the unpolished version.

The session itself is a preview of the product. It started late. It included too many introductions and a few people who were not sure they belonged on the speaker list. It handed the narrative to Dev, paused for Michelle, then handed it back. It spent real time on a game show that had not happened yet. That is not poor planning so much as community planning. The people building Miami Jam were testing the premise live: can a JavaScript open mic absorb a conference partnership without turning into a press junket? Their answer, at least in outline, is yes, if you keep the mic open, keep the questions playful, and keep the audience in the scoring loop.

Next week, Miami Jam tries that answer in public. Trivia about React, JavaScript, TypeScript, and neighboring libraries. Segues into talks, motivations, and the work that brought people to Miami. Speakers talking to speakers. Listeners asking questions and assigning points. The same JavaScript Jam Live room, with more conference gravity and a format that is allowed to be fun on purpose. If the Spaces gods cooperate, it will even start on time. If they do not, this crew has already shown they can wait a minute, laugh, and still build a show worth joining.
